title: The principle of superposition

learning_outcomes.text: explain and use the principle of superposition

external_knowledge: A wave displacement is measured from the equilibrium position and has a sign.
A displacement-position graph shows the displacement of each point at one instant.

prior_knowledge_summary: Completed Topic 7 Waves pathway: wave displacement, equilibrium position and wave graphs.
Positive and negative displacements are measured on opposite sides of equilibrium.
new_learning: Add simultaneous individual displacements algebraically at each position to obtain the resultant displacement.

blocks.heading: Two pulses try to use the same rope
content: A crest pulse moves right along a rope while a trough pulse moves left. For a moment they occupy the same section. Does one pulse block the other, or does the rope find one shared displacement?
Predict the rope shape at the instant the pulse centres meet.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a rule when two signed disturbances overlap.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with three time frames. Show a blue crest pulse and orange trough pulse approaching, overlapping, then continuing. Keep the overlap frame unlabeled so it does not reveal the prediction.
figure.alt_text: Three rope snapshots show a crest pulse and a trough pulse approaching, overlapping and moving apart.

blocks.heading: One point can receive two displacement contributions
content: Focus on one marked point P while the pulses overlap. Each pulse, considered alone, would give P a displacement from equilibrium. The rope cannot have two positions at once, so those two signed contributions combine into one resultant displacement.
The addition is local. We combine values at the same position and the same instant. We do not add a crest on the left to a trough somewhere else.

figure.purpose: Show that superposition combines simultaneous contributions at one point.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper layered sketch at point P. Draw two faint component displacement arrows from equilibrium and one bold resultant arrow. Use a vertical number line with positive upward and negative downward.
figure.alt_text: At point P, two signed component displacements combine to give one resultant displacement.

blocks.heading: The rule to learn
content: Definition to learn: when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
Here sum means algebraic sum. A downward displacement is negative, so adding it can reduce or reverse an upward displacement.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: when waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the sum of the individual displacements

figure.purpose: Connect signed arithmetic to the physical resultant.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison strip with three cases at a single point: +2 plus +1, +2 plus -1, and +2 plus -2. Show component arrows and resultant arrows with sparse labels.
figure.alt_text: Three signed-displacement examples show reinforcement, partial cancellation and complete cancellation.

blocks.heading: Build a resultant graph point by point
content: Two wave snapshots are drawn on the same position axis. At position A their displacements are +3.0 cm and +1.0 cm, so the resultant is +4.0 cm. At B they are +2.0 cm and -3.0 cm, so the resultant is -1.0 cm. At C they are -2.0 cm and -2.0 cm, so the resultant is -4.0 cm.

Repeat this signed addition at every marked position, plot each resultant value, and join the plotted points with a smooth curve. A table is often the shortest route because it prevents values from different positions being mixed.

Independent check: wherever both component curves cross equilibrium, the resultant must also be zero. Wherever the components have equal and opposite displacements, the resultant must cross equilibrium too.

figure.purpose: Teach the complete graph-construction procedure without duplicating a practice graph.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout with two small component graphs, a signed value table for A, B and C, and a separate resultant graph. Use coloured guide lines linking matching positions.
figure.alt_text: Component graph values are added in a table at matching positions and plotted to form a resultant graph.

blocks.heading: Overlap changes the observed shape, not the identity of each pulse
content: Think of two teams briefly pulling the same marked ring, one upward and one downward. The ring responds to the combined signed effect at that instant. In the same way, a point on the rope responds to both wave displacements while they overlap.
After the pulses separate, each pulse continues. Superposition describes the resultant during overlap. It does not mean that one pulse has permanently destroyed the other.

figure.purpose: Give a second causal model and distinguish temporary cancellation from pulse destruction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper before-during-after sequence. Track each pulse with a small coloured dot on its shoulder so its continuation after overlap is visible. Avoid node or interference terminology.
figure.alt_text: Two labelled pulses combine temporarily during overlap and then continue on their original paths.

blocks.heading: A flat rope does not always mean no waves
content: It feels natural to say that two equal opposite pulses disappear because the rope is momentarily flat. That conclusion uses only the resultant snapshot.

At that instant, every positive displacement from one pulse is paired with an equal negative displacement from the other, so the algebraic sum is zero. The component pulses still exist and later separate. Zero resultant displacement means cancellation at that instant, not permanent removal of both waves.

figure.purpose: Repair the belief that complete cancellation permanently removes the waves.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-layer sketch. Top shows equal opposite component pulses as faint coloured curves over a flat bold resultant. Bottom shows the two pulses separated later. Label only component and resultant.
figure.alt_text: Equal opposite pulses give a flat resultant during overlap but are shown separated again later.

blocks.heading: A reliable three-step method
content: First choose one position and read each individual displacement at the same instant. Second keep the signs and add the values algebraically. Third plot or state the resultant, then repeat at the next position if a complete graph is required.
The principle of superposition applies only where the waves overlap. It gives a resultant displacement, not a new rule for wavelength, frequency or stationary-wave structure.
Use a sketch for direction and shape, and use a signed table when several graph points must be combined.

figure.purpose: Summarise the transferable point-by-point construction method.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flow diagram: same position and instant, read signed components, add, plot resultant, repeat. Include one tiny worked point +1.5 cm plus -0.5 cm equals +1.0 cm.
figure.alt_text: A flow diagram summarises reading, adding and plotting signed displacements at matching positions.

evidence_basis.p1_status: deferred by canonical lesson specification; no lesson assignment invented

concepts_taught: point-by-point algebraic addition of signed displacements
misconceptions_addressed: A momentarily flat resultant means the component waves have permanently disappeared.
Displacements at different positions may be added together.
next_lesson_can_assume: The exact controlled definition of the principle of superposition.
Signed displacements can be added at the same position and instant.
A resultant displacement graph can be constructed point by point.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: The meanings of node and antinode.
Stationary-wave spacing relationships or experimental arrangements.
